An Iterative Dual-Channel Neural Quantum State Algorithm for Selected Configuration Interaction

Jen-Yu Chang Affiliation: Department of Electrophysics, National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University, Hsinchu, Taiwan    Yi-Chun Chang Affiliation: Arete Honors Program, National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University, Hsinchu, Taiwan    Yu-Jui Lin Affiliation: Master Program in Quantum Science and Technology, National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University, Hsinchu, Taiwan    Ming-Chun Yang Affiliation: Department of Electrophysics, National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University, Hsinchu, Taiwan    Hsiu-Chi Tsai Affiliation: Arete Honors Program, National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University, Hsinchu, Taiwan    Tai-Yue Li Affiliation: National Center for High-performance Computing, National Institutes of Applied Research, Hsinchu, Taiwan    Nan Yow Chen Affiliation: National Center for High-performance Computing, National Institutes of Applied Research, Hsinchu, Taiwan    Tsung-Wei Huang Affiliation: Quantum Information Center, Chung Yuan Christian University, Taoyuan, Taiwan Affiliation: Master Program in Intelligent Computing and Big Data, Chung Yuan Christian University, Taoyuan, Taiwan    En-Jui Kuo Affiliation: Department of Electrophysics, National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University, Hsinchu, Taiwan Affiliation: Corresponding author. Abstract

Accurately solving the electronic Schrödinger equation for strongly correlated systems remains a central challenge in quantum chemistry, where the exponential growth of configuration space limits the applicability of exact methods. Selected Configuration Interaction (SCI) algorithms address this challenge by adaptively constructing compact determinantal expansions, yet their efficiency depends critically on the quality of the sampling strategy used to identify chemically important configurations. Here we introduce the Handover Iterative Neural Quantum State (HI-NQS) algorithm, which embeds a classically trained autoregressive Transformer neural quantum state within the iterative sample–diagonalize–update framework of Sample-Based Quantum Diagonalization. A dual-channel Transformer architecture with explicit spin-up/spin-down cross-attention encodes fermionic spin structure as an architectural inductive bias, enabling expressive and physically informed wavefunction representations. After each subspace diagonalization, the resulting eigenvector is distilled back into the network through a factorized spin-marginal teacher signal, establishing a closed feedback loop between generative sampling and exact diagonalization. Benchmarks across a range of small molecules and a systematic nitrogen active-space series demonstrate that HI-NQS achieves chemical accuracy on all systems tested, with determinant-count scaling substantially more favorable than conventional CIPSI-based SCI for all but the smallest active spaces. All calculations are performed on GPU hardware without quantum computing resources, establishing HI-NQS as an efficient and scalable purely classical approach to the selected configuration interaction problem.

1 Introduction

Accurately computing the ground-state energy of strongly correlated molecular systems is a central challenge of ab initio quantum chemistry, because the many-body Hilbert space grows exponentially with system size. Full Configuration Interaction (FCI) expands the wavefunction on the complete Slater-determinant basis 45 and is therefore intractable beyond small active spaces, a bottleneck that has driven a succession of reduction strategies on both classical and quantum hardware.

On the classical side, SCI algorithms 18, 17, 40, 48, 37 retain only the most energetically important determinants, iteratively growing the basis through excitation-based candidate generation and perturbative screening. Complementary approaches include the density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) 5, which reaches high accuracy for quasi-one-dimensional correlation topologies, and FCI Quantum Monte Carlo (FCIQMC) 3, which samples the complete determinant space stochastically without explicit enumeration. Modern SCI variants reach chemical accuracy on small-to-medium active spaces, but their candidate pool grows combinatorially with excitation rank, and the subspace diagonalization that follows scales cubically in basis size—limiting their reach into strongly correlated regimes where the relevant basis must grow rapidly.

Quantum hardware has motivated a parallel lineage. The Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) 32, 29 and its adaptive variants such as ADAPT-VQE 14 parameterize the wavefunction through a circuit, but barren plateaus 28, 25, measurement overheads that already reach 10910^{9}–101010^{10} shots for small molecules at chemical accuracy 51, 13, and irreducible gate noise render it impractical at scale. Sample-Based Quantum Diagonalization (SQD) 35, 56 and the related quantum-selected configuration interaction (QSCI) scheme 20 addressed these costs with a hybrid strategy: the quantum device samples bitstrings from the circuit distribution, while a classical computer constructs the second-quantized Hamiltonian restricted to that sampled subspace and diagonalizes it exactly. This separation reduces the measurement burden substantially, but each invocation of the quantum sampler remains a one-shot procedure with no mechanism to refine the sampled subspace across calls.

Handover Iterative VQE (HI-VQE) 31, 55 formalized and extended this hybrid strategy into the handover principle—the defining idea captured in its name: the quantum device is responsible solely for proposing configurations, and all energy evaluation is permanently handed over to classical exact diagonalization. Crucially, HI-VQE closes a feedback loop: after each subspace diagonalization, the resulting eigenvector is fed back to update the variational circuit parameters, concentrating subsequent sampling on the most energetically relevant configurations. This iterative sample–diagonalize–update cycle converges to chemical accuracy on systems such as N2 and Fe–S clusters with shot counts substantially below those of standard VQE.

A parallel line attempts to realize the same selection-plus-feedback idea using classical Neural Quantum States (NQS) 4, 33, 15, 7, 24, which encode the wavefunction implicitly in network parameters. Pure NQS variational Monte Carlo (VMC), however, relies on Stochastic Reconfiguration 42, whose Fisher-matrix inversion scales as 𝒪⁡(P3)\mathcal{O}(P^{3}) for PP parameters 26, 6, and —more fundamentally—provides no external accuracy anchor: whatever energy the network converges to, there is no mechanism to diagnose or correct its residual variational bias. Two complementary families of neural-network-augmented SCI close this gap by adding an external scoring or diagonalization step. The first is discriminative: Neural-Network Configuration Interaction (NNCI) 36, 2, 46, extending earlier neural-network-driven CI selection 8, 16, trains a convolutional classifier via active learning to score determinants drawn from an externally enumerated single- and double-excitation pool, reproducing the N2 correlation energy with ∼×105\sim\!4\!\times\!10^{5} determinants in a 52-orbital active space where the underlying FCI dimension exceeds 101010^{10}. Being a classifier over an externally enumerated pool, NNCI’s reachable configuration space is tied to the excitation rank used to build that pool, and its 1D-CNN architecture treats the occupation vector as a single α\alpha-then-β\beta concatenated sequence with no cross-channel attention between the spin-up and spin-down blocks.

The second family is generative: an NQS is trained to sample candidate determinants directly from a learned Born distribution, with the CI subspace diagonalization providing the external accuracy anchor. Five recent methods fall in this family:

  • •

    QiankunNet-cuSCI 43 (built on the QiankunNet Transformer NQS framework 53, 38): GPU-accelerated NQS+SCI scaling to active spaces of up to 84 qubits (Cr2); the Transformer is trained by variational energy minimization and candidates are proposed through GPU-kernel-accelerated Hamiltonian excitation enumeration.

  • •

    NQS-SC 41: neural-backflow ansatz on a selected-configuration subspace; energy minimization on the selected space, with new candidates drawn from the H^\hat{H}-connected expansion H^​𝒮select\hat{H}\,\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{select}}.

  • •

    HAAR-SCI 58: gated Transformer that samples determinants autoregressively with Gumbel Top-KK 23 exploration; trained by regression to Lanczos eigenvector amplitudes, with GPU min-heap kernels retaining only configurations with the largest Hamiltonian couplings.

  • •

    ARNN-SCI 47: masked-autoregressive dense (MADE-style 12) network trained by maximum likelihood on configurations sampled from each iteration’s SCI eigenvector; new configurations are then proposed by direct autoregressive sampling.

  • •

    GTNN-SCI 19 (also built on QiankunNet 53, 38): generative Transformer regressed to CI eigenvector amplitudes; operates in two phases, transitioning from Hamiltonian-guided candidate scoring to direct autoregressive sampling once the learned distribution is sufficiently sharp.

These methods confirm that generative NQS sampling and CI subspace diagonalization are synergistic; three of them (HAAR-SCI 58, ARNN-SCI 47, GTNN-SCI 19) already feed CI eigenvector information back into the NQS through supervised losses. Their shared architectural limitation, however, is that all of these networks—whether a backflow ansatz (NQS-SC), a single-stream Transformer (QiankunNet-cuSCI, HAAR-SCI, GTNN-SCI), or a masked-dense ARNN (ARNN-SCI)—process the α\alpha and β\beta spin-orbital indices as positions in a single sequence, with no dedicated cross-channel attention between the spin-up and spin-down subsystems.

We propose HI-NQS, which adopts the handover loop of HI-VQE 31, 55 as its architectural backbone, substitutes the quantum-circuit sampler with a classically trained autoregressive Transformer NQS, and retains SQD as the classical subspace solver. Building on the second-quantized autoregressive ansatz 1, 39—which factorizes the Born distribution πθ​(𝐱)=∏ipθ​(xi∣x<i)\pi_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})=\prod_{i}p_{\theta}(x_{i}\mid x_{<i}) to enable exact ancestral sampling under hard particle-number constraints—we choose a Transformer rather than a recurrent or backflow backbone for two practical reasons: its conditionals are evaluable in parallel in a single forward pass, and its self-attention mechanism extends naturally to the cross-channel coupling described next. The first architectural element is a dual-channel design in which a spin-α\alpha stream of causal self-attention layers is coupled to a spin-β\beta stream via cross-attention to the full α\alpha configuration, making the α\alpha/β\beta separation of second-quantized fermions an explicit architectural prior rather than one the network must learn from data; this contrasts directly with the single-stream encodings of all five generative baselines and with NNCI’s concatenated 1D-CNN encoding.

The second contribution lies in how the network is trained and how it explores configuration space. After each SQD diagonalization, the resulting eigenvector Ψ0\Psi_{0} is distilled into the NQS through a teacher signal given by the factorized product of its spin-resolved marginals, pα​(σα)​pβ​(σβ)p_{\alpha}(\sigma^{\alpha})\,p_{\beta}(\sigma^{\beta}), optimized with exactly backpropagated gradients rather than by energy minimization alone. Three of the generative baselines above (HAAR-SCI, ARNN-SCI, GTNN-SCI) already employ supervised losses against CI amplitudes; the contribution here is the factorization of that target into per-spin-channel marginals, which is architecturally consistent with the two-channel network of the preceding paragraph and turns the dual-channel cross-attention into an actively supervised pathway rather than a passive structural prior. A deterministic classical expansion of single and double excitations of the dominant determinants in the current basis is added in parallel with the NQS proposals to counteract the mode collapse 27 that afflicts autoregressive samplers at late iterations and to guarantee a steady supply of fresh determinants in the H^\hat{H}-connected vicinity of the high-amplitude region. Benchmarks on an eight-point N2 active-space series sweeping CAS(6,6) through CAS(14,20) (12 to 40 qubits, cc-pVDZ) together with ten small molecules at 12–30 qubits demonstrate that HI-NQS attains chemical accuracy (|E−Eref|<1.6|E-E_{\mathrm{ref}}|<1.6 mHa) on all eighteen systems, with the N2 variational basis growing from ∼×104\sim\!4\!\times\!10^{4} determinants at CAS(14,14) to ∼×105\sim\!1.7\!\times\!10^{5} at CAS(14,20) (40 qubits)—roughly 200×200\times (≈2.3\approx 2.3 orders of magnitude) fewer than CIPSI-SCI at the largest active space, and yielding a log-linear scaling exponent αNQS=0.089±0.011\alpha_{\mathrm{NQS}}=0.089\pm 0.011 in NdetN_{\mathrm{det}} versus qubit count, roughly half that of CIPSI-SCI (αCIPSI=0.180\alpha_{\mathrm{CIPSI}}=0.180) and a third that of complete active-space CI (CASCI; αCASCI=0.262\alpha_{\mathrm{CASCI}}=0.262). At 40 qubits HI-NQS requires ∼200×\sim\!200\times fewer determinants than CIPSI-SCI while matching or exceeding its accuracy, all on commodity GPU hardware without quantum resources.

2 Method

The HI-NQS algorithm iterates between six stages: (i) an autoregressive Transformer NQS that proposes candidate Slater determinants; (i′) a deterministic classical expansion that enumerates single and double excitations of the dominant determinants in the current basis, counteracting mode collapse of the autoregressive sampler; (ii) a perturbation-theory scoring stage that selects the most energetically relevant configurations from the combined candidate pool; (iii) an SQD diagonalization that yields an updated ground-state energy and eigenvector; (iv) a supervised update in which the SQD eigenvector is distilled back into the NQS as a teacher signal; and (v) a convergence check that terminates the loop once the variational energy has stabilized. After variational convergence, the converged energy EvarE_{\mathrm{var}} is a strict upper bound to the exact energy and is the quantity reported throughout this work; no post-processing PT2 correction is applied, because the Epstein–Nesbet 10, 30 correction is non-variational—it can push the total energy below the exact FCI ground state at insufficient basis sizes—and CIPSI-SCI likewise reports bare variational energies, placing both methods on equal footing. Each component is described in the following subsections.

2.1 Neural quantum state architecture

We represent the electronic wavefunction with an autoregressive Transformer 49—related self-attention ansätze in first-quantized molecular electronic structure include Psiformer 50—that models the joint probability distribution over occupation-number strings 𝐱=(x1,x2,…,x2​M)\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{2M}), where MM is the number of spatial orbitals and each xi∈{0,1}x_{i}\in\{0,1\} indicates whether spin-orbital ii is occupied. We organize the occupation string into a spin-α\alpha sub-string σα=(x1α,…,xMα)\sigma^{\alpha}=(x_{1}^{\alpha},\ldots,x_{M}^{\alpha}) and a spin-β\beta sub-string σβ=(x1β,…,xMβ)\sigma^{\beta}=(x_{1}^{\beta},\ldots,x_{M}^{\beta}), so that 𝐱=(σα,σβ)\mathbf{x}=(\sigma^{\alpha},\sigma^{\beta}), and factorize the Born distribution as

πθ​(𝐱)=∏i=1Mpθ​(xiα∣x<iα)​∏j=1Mpθ​(xjβ∣x<jβ,σα),\pi_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})=\prod_{i=1}^{M}p_{\theta}(x_{i}^{\alpha}\mid x_{<i}^{\alpha})\;\prod_{j=1}^{M}p_{\theta}(x_{j}^{\beta}\mid x_{<j}^{\beta},\,\sigma^{\alpha}), (1)

an exact chain-rule factorization in which the β\beta conditionals depend on the full α\alpha sub-string. This autoregressive form is chosen so that (i) πθ​(𝐱)\pi_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) is normalized by construction and log⁡πθ\log\pi_{\theta} admits an analytic, partition-function-free evaluation; (ii) configurations can be drawn as independent samples by sequential conditional sampling, without Markov-chain mixing or rejection; and (iii) discrete symmetries such as particle-number conservation can be imposed exactly at the level of each conditional, as described below. Together these three properties—exact log-probabilities, unbiased samples, and built-in symmetry—are precisely what the perturbative selection step of Sec. 2.2.3 and the supervised update of Sec. 2.2.5 require, and they motivate the autoregressive architecture detailed below in preference to Markov-chain-based neural ansätze.

The two factors in Eq. (1) are parameterized by two dedicated Transformer streams, which we refer to as the α\alpha channel and the β\beta channel (Fig. 1). The α\alpha channel is a stack of LαL_{\alpha} pre-LayerNorm 54 Transformer blocks with causal (masked) multi-head self-attention that generates the spin-up conditionals pθ​(xiα∣x<iα)p_{\theta}(x_{i}^{\alpha}\mid x_{<i}^{\alpha}). The full sampled σα\sigma^{\alpha} is then re-encoded through the same α\alpha weights without the causal mask to produce a bidirectional contextual representation 𝐇α∈ℝM×dmodel\mathbf{H}^{\alpha}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times d_{\mathrm{model}}}, which we refer to as the α\alpha-context. The β\beta channel is a second stack of LβL_{\beta} Transformer blocks, each of which augments causal self-attention over previously sampled β\beta positions with cross-attention to the α\alpha-context 𝐇α\mathbf{H}^{\alpha}, so that each β\beta conditional has access to the complete α\alpha configuration. Each output head produces a single logit per position, passed through a sigmoid to yield pθ(xi=1∣⋅)p_{\theta}(x_{i}=1\mid\cdot), so that log⁡πθ​(𝐱)\log\pi_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) can be evaluated in parallel over all positions in a single forward pass via binary cross-entropy with logits.

Particle-number symmetry is enforced during autoregressive sampling rather than by post-hoc rejection. At each sampling step ii the logit ℓi\ell_{i} is clipped to a large positive value whenever the remaining sites in the current spin channel must all be occupied to reach the target electron count, and to a large negative value whenever the target has already been saturated. Every drawn configuration therefore satisfies ∑ixiα=nαe\sum_{i}x_{i}^{\alpha}=n_{\alpha}^{e} and ∑ixiβ=nβe\sum_{i}x_{i}^{\beta}=n_{\beta}^{e} by construction; a residual particle-number filter is retained only as a numerical safety net. Fixing (nαe,nβe)(n_{\alpha}^{e},n_{\beta}^{e}) separately also fixes the total spin projection Sz=(nαe−nβe)/2S_{z}=(n_{\alpha}^{e}-n_{\beta}^{e})/2; S^2\hat{S}^{2} is not constrained at the ansatz level and is resolved by the subsequent subspace diagonalization.

2.2 Iterative handover loop

Given a second-quantized molecular Hamiltonian H^=∑p​qhp​q​a^p†​a^q+12​∑p​q​r​sgp​q​r​s​a^p†​a^q†​a^s​a^r+Enuc\hat{H}=\sum_{pq}h_{pq}\,\hat{a}_{p}^{\dagger}\hat{a}_{q}+\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{pqrs}g_{pqrs}\,\hat{a}_{p}^{\dagger}\hat{a}_{q}^{\dagger}\hat{a}_{s}\hat{a}_{r}+E_{\mathrm{nuc}} in an orthonormal orbital basis, the algorithm proceeds as follows (Fig. 2).

2.2.1 Step 1: NQS sampling

At iteration tt the NQS draws NsN_{s} occupation strings autoregressively [Eq. (1)] at a temperature T⁡(t)T(t) that is annealed linearly from T0=1.0T_{0}=1.0 to Tmin=0.3T_{\min}=0.3 over the course of the run. The schedule biases early iterations toward broader exploration and later iterations toward the peak of the learned Born distribution. Configurations duplicating entries of the cumulative basis ℬ\mathcal{B} are removed, yielding a set of NQS-proposed candidates 𝒞tNQS\mathcal{C}_{t}^{\mathrm{NQS}}.

2.2.2 Step 1′: Classical expansion

In addition to the stochastic NQS proposals, a deterministic expansion is performed every iteration once an eigenvector is available (t≥1t\geq 1). Let ℬtop(Ne)⊂ℬ\mathcal{B}_{\text{top}}^{(N_{e})}\subset\mathcal{B} denote the NeN_{e} basis determinants with the largest amplitudes |ci||c_{i}| in the current eigenvector Ψ0\Psi_{0}. We enumerate every singly and doubly excited determinant connected to any element of ℬtop(Ne)\mathcal{B}_{\text{top}}^{(N_{e})} by a non-zero Hamiltonian matrix element,

𝒞tcl={𝐲∉ℬ:∃𝐱∈ℬtop(Ne),⟨𝐲|H^|𝐱⟩≠0},\mathcal{C}_{t}^{\mathrm{cl}}=\big\{\,\mathbf{y}\notin\mathcal{B}\,:\,\exists\,\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{B}_{\text{top}}^{(N_{e})},\;\langle\mathbf{y}|\hat{H}|\mathbf{x}\rangle\neq 0\,\big\}, (2)

and merge 𝒞tcl\mathcal{C}_{t}^{\mathrm{cl}} with 𝒞tNQS\mathcal{C}_{t}^{\mathrm{NQS}} to form the full candidate pool 𝒞t=𝒞tNQS∪𝒞tcl\mathcal{C}_{t}=\mathcal{C}_{t}^{\mathrm{NQS}}\cup\mathcal{C}_{t}^{\mathrm{cl}}. This step compensates for the gradual collapse of πθ\pi_{\theta} onto high-amplitude regions of ℬ\mathcal{B} at later iterations: even when the NQS proposal distribution becomes peaked, the classical expansion guarantees a steady supply of fresh determinants in the H^\hat{H}-connected vicinity of the dominant amplitudes. We use Ne=1000N_{e}=1000 throughout this work.

2.2.3 Step 2: Configuration scoring and basis update

Candidates are ranked by their expected contribution to the ground-state energy, and the cumulative basis ℬ\mathcal{B} is updated accordingly. The ranking criterion depends on whether an approximate eigenvector is available from a previous diagonalization.

Iteration t=0t=0 (cold start).

No eigenvector Ψ0\Psi_{0} is yet available. Candidates are ranked by their diagonal Hamiltonian matrix element H𝐱𝐱=⟨𝐱|H^|𝐱⟩H_{\mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}}=\langle\mathbf{x}|\hat{H}|\mathbf{x}\rangle. The K0K_{0} lowest-energy candidates form the initial basis ℬ\mathcal{B}, with the cold-start budget K0K_{0} chosen no larger than the per-iteration budget KK used in later iterations.

Iteration t=1t=1 (full rescore).

Once the first eigenvector Ψ0\Psi_{0} is available, both existing entries in ℬ\mathcal{B} and new candidates 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} are rescored using the Epstein–Nesbet second-order perturbation theory (PT2) importance measure

s⁡(𝐱)=|⟨𝐱|H^|Ψ0⟩|2|E0−H𝐱𝐱|,s(\mathbf{x})=\frac{|\langle\mathbf{x}|\hat{H}|\Psi_{0}\rangle|^{2}}{|E_{0}-H_{\mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}}|}, (3)

where the coupling ⟨𝐱|H^|Ψ0⟩=∑ici​H𝐱,𝐱i\langle\mathbf{x}|\hat{H}|\Psi_{0}\rangle=\sum_{i}c_{i}\,H_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}_{i}} is evaluated over the eigenvector coefficients {ci}\{c_{i}\} and basis determinants {𝐱i}\{\mathbf{x}_{i}\}. The absolute value in the denominator makes s⁡(𝐱)≥0s(\mathbf{x})\geq 0 a magnitude-only ranking criterion. The basis is then rebuilt from scratch: ℬ\mathcal{B} is replaced by the top KK configurations ranked by s⁡(𝐱)s(\mathbf{x}). The hard cap ℬmax\mathcal{B}_{\max} is not applied at this step so that every cold-start determinant—which was selected by a weaker diagonal criterion—receives at least one PT2 evaluation before being eligible for eviction.

Iterations t≥2t\geq 2 (incremental update).

Only new candidates 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t} are scored via Eq. (3); the top KK are appended to ℬ\mathcal{B}. If |ℬ|>ℬmax|\mathcal{B}|>\mathcal{B}_{\max}, the lowest-scored entries are evicted.

2.2.4 Step 3: Subspace diagonalization

The projected Hamiltonian HℬH_{\mathcal{B}} with matrix elements [Hℬ]i​j=⟨𝐱i|H^|𝐱j⟩[H_{\mathcal{B}}]_{ij}=\langle\mathbf{x}_{i}|\hat{H}|\mathbf{x}_{j}\rangle is constructed and diagonalized with a Davidson eigensolver 9. By default we use an incremental SQD backend that persists a PySCF 44 selected_ci state across iterations and warm-starts Davidson from the previous eigenvector, with IBM’s solve_fermion routine 35 retained as a fallback. This yields the total ground-state energy E0=Ecorr+EnucE_{0}=E_{\mathrm{corr}}+E_{\mathrm{nuc}} in the selected subspace and the corresponding eigenvector Ψ0\Psi_{0} expressed as a linear combination of the basis determinants. Because this step is an exact diagonalization within ℬ\mathcal{B}, E0E_{0} is variational with respect to the selected subspace.

2.2.5 Step 4: NQS update

The NQS is retrained to reflect the eigenvector Ψ0\Psi_{0} obtained in Step 3. Training uses a composite loss

ℒtotal=wteach​ℒteacher+wener​ℒenergy+wentr​ℒentropy,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{total}}=w_{\mathrm{teach}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{teacher}}+w_{\mathrm{ener}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{energy}}+w_{\mathrm{entr}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{entropy}}, (4)

whose components are defined below.

Teacher weights.

We compute spin-resolved marginals of |Ψ0|2|\Psi_{0}|^{2},

pα​(σα)\displaystyle p_{\alpha}(\sigma^{\alpha}) =∑σβ|Ψ0​(σα,σβ)|2,\displaystyle=\sum_{\sigma^{\beta}}|\Psi_{0}(\sigma^{\alpha},\sigma^{\beta})|^{2}, (5)
pβ​(σβ)\displaystyle p_{\beta}(\sigma^{\beta}) =∑σα|Ψ0​(σα,σβ)|2,\displaystyle=\sum_{\sigma^{\alpha}}|\Psi_{0}(\sigma^{\alpha},\sigma^{\beta})|^{2}, (6)

and assign each basis configuration 𝐱=(σα,σβ)\mathbf{x}=(\sigma^{\alpha},\sigma^{\beta}) the factorized teacher weight w⁡(𝐱)=pα​(σα)​pβ​(σβ)w(\mathbf{x})=p_{\alpha}(\sigma^{\alpha})\,p_{\beta}(\sigma^{\beta}), normalized so that ∑𝐱∈ℬw⁡(𝐱)=1\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{B}}w(\mathbf{x})=1. This factorized form discards the phase of Ψ0\Psi_{0} and the residual α\alpha–β\beta correlation of |Ψ0|2|\Psi_{0}|^{2}.

Loss components.

The three terms are

ℒteacher\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{teacher}} =−∑𝐱∈ℬw(𝐱)logπθ(𝐱),\displaystyle=-\!\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{B}}w(\mathbf{x})\,\log\pi_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}), (7)
ℒenergy\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{energy}} =∑𝐱∈ℬw⁡(𝐱)​A​(𝐱)​log⁡πθ​(𝐱),\displaystyle=\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{B}}w(\mathbf{x})\,A(\mathbf{x})\,\log\pi_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}), (8)
ℒentropy\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{entropy}} =1|ℬ|​∑𝐱∈ℬlog⁡πθ​(𝐱),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{B}|}\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{B}}\log\pi_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}), (9)

where A⁡(𝐱)=H𝐱𝐱−E0A(\mathbf{x})=H_{\mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}}-E_{0} is the single-determinant advantage relative to the current ground-state energy. ℒteacher\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{teacher}} is the cross-entropy between the teacher weights w⁡(𝐱)w(\mathbf{x}) and πθ​(𝐱)\pi_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) evaluated on ℬ\mathcal{B}. ℒenergy\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{energy}} is a REINFORCE-style policy-gradient 52 term that raises log⁡πθ​(𝐱)\log\pi_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) for A<0A<0 and lowers it for A>0A>0. ℒentropy\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{entropy}} is an anti-concentration regularizer: minimizing it lowers the average log-probability on ℬ\mathcal{B}, redistributing probability mass toward configurations outside the current basis. Gradients are computed on mini-batches of size min⁡(5000,|ℬ|)\min(5000,|\mathcal{B}|) and clipped to a maximum norm of 1.01.0; parameter updates use Adam 21 with exactly backpropagated gradients.

2.2.6 Step 5: Convergence

The variational loop terminates when the energy change |E0(t)−E0(t−1)||E_{0}^{(t)}-E_{0}^{(t-1)}| falls below a threshold δ=10−9​Ha\delta=10^{-9}\,\mathrm{Ha} for five consecutive iterations, or when a maximum number of iterations is reached. We use a maximum of 5050 iterations throughout this work. We denote the converged variational energy by Evar≡limt→∞E0(t)E_{\mathrm{var}}\equiv\lim_{t\to\infty}E_{0}^{(t)}.

3 Results and Discussion

Across 18 benchmark systems spanning 1212–4040 qubits, HI-NQS attains chemical accuracy on every system tested, with a log-linear NdetN_{\mathrm{det}} scaling exponent of αNQS=0.089±0.011\alpha_{\mathrm{NQS}}=0.089\pm 0.011—half that of CIPSI-SCI (αCIPSI=0.180\alpha_{\mathrm{CIPSI}}=0.180) and a third that of CASCI (αCASCI=0.262\alpha_{\mathrm{CASCI}}=0.262, Fig. 3). At the largest active space tested (CAS(14,20), 40 qubits) this compounds to a ∼200×\sim\!200\times (≈2.3\approx 2.3 orders of magnitude) determinant reduction relative to CIPSI-SCI.

We benchmark HI-NQS against CIPSI-SCI (implemented via PySCF’s selected_ci module 44, 18) and, where tractable, against the exact FCI limit on two families: ten small molecules at 1212–3030 qubits (Group A) and a single N2 active-space series, CAS(6,6) through CAS(14,20), spanning 1212–4040 qubits in the cc-pVDZ basis (Group B). For each method we report its natural-convergence determinant count NdetN_{\mathrm{det}}: the smallest basis (ordered by size) from which the energy stays within 0.10.1 mHa of its own converged plateau. This self-convergence criterion is applied identically to CIPSI-SCI and to the NQS variational basis, so the two are compared at matched convergence rather than against a fixed external target. Both methods report bare variational energies: CIPSI uses the subspace-diagonalization energy at its converged iteration, and NQS reports EvarE_{\mathrm{var}} (no Epstein–Nesbet PT2 correction), a strict upper bound to the exact energy. Reference energies are exact FCI for seventeen of the eighteen systems (Eref=EFCIE_{\mathrm{ref}}=E_{\mathrm{FCI}}), computed with PySCF’s Davidson FCI solver (pyscf.fci.direct_spin1). The sole exception is N2-CAS(14,20) (40 qubits, ∼6×109\sim\!6\times 10^{9} determinants), where exact FCI is computationally infeasible; we substitute a Dice semistochastic heat-bath CI (SHCI)+det-PT2 reference 17, 40 (heat-bath variational selection with deterministic Epstein–Nesbet PT2), Eref=EvarSHCI+EPT2E_{\mathrm{ref}}=E_{\mathrm{var}}^{\mathrm{SHCI}}+E_{\mathrm{PT2}}, converged across a seven-point cutoff sweep ε∈[10−3,10−6]\varepsilon\in[10^{-3},10^{-6}]. Selected configuration-interaction at this cutoff is generally converged to within ≲10−5\lesssim 10^{-5} Ha of exact FCI, two orders below the 1.6×10−31.6\times 10^{-3} Ha chemical-accuracy scale of any quantitative claim in this work. NQS energies are averaged over three seeds in Table 1 and Fig. 3, and over ten seeds in Fig. 4 (median ±\pm IQR). Table 1 collects the comparison.

Small molecules (Group A). All ten systems reach chemical accuracy, |E−Eref|<1.6|E-E_{\mathrm{ref}}|<1.6 mHa, with both methods, and the NQS variational basis is more compact than CIPSI-SCI on all ten. The gains are largest for the weakly correlated cases—H2S (0.066×0.066\times, a 15×15\times reduction), BeH2 (0.24×0.24\times), and N2 (0.27×0.27\times)—and remain substantial for the more strongly correlated systems: HCN and C2H2 (0.53×0.53\times each), H2O (0.55×0.55\times), C2H4 (0.56×0.56\times), and NH3 (0.42×0.42\times). The smallest advantage is LiH (0.91×0.91\times), where the dominant determinants are few and both methods converge at near-identical basis sizes. All ten NQS variational energies lie above the exact FCI (Δ​ENQS≥0\Delta E_{\mathrm{NQS}}\geq 0), with the largest overshoot +0.099+0.099 mHa at C2H2—well within chemical accuracy.

Active-space scaling (Group B). The N2 series isolates the size dependence. Figure 3 plots NdetN_{\mathrm{det}} at convergence against qubit count; all three methods grow log-linearly, log10⁡Ndet≈αX​nq+βX\log_{10}N_{\mathrm{det}}\approx\alpha_{X}\,n_{q}+\beta_{X}, with the NQS exponent roughly half that of CIPSI-SCI and a third that of full CASCI (fitted values in Fig. 3 caption). The determinant advantage is therefore not a constant prefactor but compounds with active-space size: from parity at CAS(6,6) (both methods saturate the 400400-determinant FCI space) the NQS/CIPSI ratio falls monotonically through 0.300.30 at CAS(10,10), 0.0360.036 at CAS(14,14), to 5.0×10−35.0\times 10^{-3} at CAS(14,20)—a ∼200×\sim\!200\times (≈2.3\approx 2.3 orders of magnitude) determinant reduction relative to CIPSI-SCI, and ∼4.5\sim\!4.5 orders below the full CASCI dimension, at 4040 qubits (for context, the current frontier of distributed FCI implementations reaches the trillion-determinant scale 11). For CAS(14,16) and CAS(14,18) the reference is exact PySCF FCI on Hilbert spaces of 1.3×1081.3\times 10^{8} and 1.0×1091.0\times 10^{9} determinants, respectively; for CAS(14,20) (6.0×1096.0\times 10^{9} determinants) exact FCI is infeasible at single-node scale and we substitute a Dice-SHCI+det-PT2 estimate at ε=10−6\varepsilon=10^{-6} as an FCI proxy; see caption of Table 1 for details. The NNQS/NCIPSIN_{\mathrm{NQS}}/N_{\mathrm{CIPSI}} ratios in Table 1 therefore compare two independent natural-convergence picks at every qubit count.

Accuracy–cost Pareto front. Figure 4 shows the full trade-off for four representative sizes (CAS(10,10), (14,14), (14,18), and (14,20)). At every active space shown, the NQS curve lies to the left of the CIPSI-SCI sweep—it reaches any given accuracy with fewer determinants—and the horizontal separation widens monotonically from CAS(10,10) to CAS(14,20), the per-system manifestation of the exponent gap in Fig. 3. At the largest active spaces both curves approach a sub-mHa accuracy floor; all NQS variational energies sit above their respective references, consistent with the variational upper-bound property of EvarE_{\mathrm{var}}.

A monotonically size-dependent advantage. Taken together, the data show that the NQS compactness gain is present across the full benchmark and grows monotonically with active-space size. On 13 of the 18 systems this advantage is Pareto-dominant: HI-NQS uses fewer determinants and lands at least as close to the reference (bold entries in Table 1); on the four remaining small molecules (BeH2, N2, C2H2, H2S) it is still more compact but slightly less accurate, its energy trailing CIPSI by less than 0.10.1 mHa and always within chemical accuracy. The sole neutral point in the entire benchmark is CAS(6,6), where both methods saturate the 400400-determinant FCI space. Across Group A the advantage ranges from near-parity at LiH (0.91×0.91\times) to 15×15\times at H2S, with NQS more compact on all ten systems. In Group B the NQS/CIPSI ratio falls continuously from 0.840.84 at CAS(8,8) through 0.0360.036 at CAS(14,14) to 5.0×10−35.0\times 10^{-3} at CAS(14,20). The learned, physics-supervised NQS sampler concentrates amplitude into a compact support that grows far more slowly (αNQS=0.089\alpha_{\mathrm{NQS}}=0.089) than CIPSI’s perturbatively ordered expansion (αCIPSI=0.180\alpha_{\mathrm{CIPSI}}=0.180); the compactness gain is thus a scaling phenomenon that becomes decisive precisely in the strongly correlated, large-active-space regime these methods target.

Relation to other generative neural selected-CI. HI-NQS shares the generative selected-CI strategy of several recent neural ansätze—QiankunNet-cuSCI 43, NQS-SC 41, HAAR-SCI 58, ARNN-SCI 47 and GTNN-SCI 19—all of which sample determinants from a learned distribution and diagonalize the selected subspace. It differs in the two architectural respects developed in Sec. 2: a dual-channel α/β\alpha/\beta Transformer whose β\beta stream cross-attends to the full α\alpha configuration, encoding opposite-spin correlation as an explicit inductive bias rather than as a single flattened occupation string; and a supervised distillation loss that feeds the exact subspace eigenvector back through a factorized spin-marginal teacher. We attribute the shallow determinant-scaling exponent reported here to this combination, although a controlled head-to-head on identical active spaces—not recoverable from the published numbers of those works—would be required to isolate each contribution.

Limitations. Several caveats bound these claims. Table 1 reports the bare variational NQS energy EvarE_{\mathrm{var}} (no PT2 correction), which is a strict upper bound to the exact energy. Consequently Δ​ENQS≥0\Delta E_{\mathrm{NQS}}\geq 0 on every exact-FCI reference row (seventeen of the eighteen systems), with the largest deviation +0.099+0.099 mHa at C2H2—within chemical accuracy. The sole non-exact-FCI row—N2-CAS(14,20) (Dice-SHCI+det-PT2 proxy at ε=10−6\varepsilon=10^{-6})—also has positive Δ​ENQS\Delta E_{\mathrm{NQS}} (+0.041+0.041 mHa) against the substitute reference; since selected configuration-interaction at this cutoff is generally converged to within ≲10−5\lesssim 10^{-5} Ha of exact FCI 17, 40, the chemical-accuracy claim is unaffected. The CAS(14,20) row caps the verifiable accuracy of any method at the proxy’s residual (∼10−5\sim\!10^{-5} Ha), still two orders below our chemical-accuracy claim. The autoregressive sampler is prone to late-iteration mode collapse, which the deterministic single/double classical expansion mitigates but does not eliminate; and total spin S2S^{2} is not constrained at the ansatz level, being restored only by the subspace diagonalization. Finally, all benchmarks are at a single molecular geometry; dissociation curves and broken-symmetry transition-metal systems remain to be tested.

4 Conclusion

We have introduced HI-NQS, a handover iterative algorithm that replaces the quantum-circuit sampler of HI-VQE 31, 55 with a classically trained autoregressive Transformer and retains SQD 35 as the exact classical subspace solver. The two defining architectural elements—a dual-channel α\alpha/β\beta cross-attention architecture that encodes opposite-spin correlation as an explicit inductive bias, and a supervised distillation loop that feeds each SQD eigenvector back into the network through a factorized spin-marginal teacher signal—together close the feedback loop between generative sampling and exact diagonalization that open-loop NQS+SCI methods leave open. A deterministic classical expansion of single and double excitations of the dominant determinants is run in parallel with the NQS proposals to ensure a steady supply of fresh configurations in the H^\hat{H}-connected neighborhood at late iterations.

Benchmarks on ten small molecules and an eight-point N2\text{N}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}} active-space series demonstrate that this design yields a systematic and compounding computational advantage over CIPSI-SCI 18. HI-NQS achieves chemical accuracy on all ten Group A systems and on the full Group B active-space series up to CAS(14,20), while the log-linear scaling exponent of the required determinant count, αNQS=0.089±0.011\alpha_{\mathrm{NQS}}=0.089\pm 0.011, is roughly half that of CIPSI-SCI (αCIPSI=0.180\alpha_{\mathrm{CIPSI}}=0.180) and a third that of CASCI (αCASCI=0.262\alpha_{\mathrm{CASCI}}=0.262). At 40 qubits, HI-NQS requires roughly 200×200\times (≈2.3\approx 2.3 orders of magnitude) fewer determinants than CIPSI-SCI and approximately 4.54.5 orders of magnitude fewer than the full CASCI Hilbert space, with HI-NQS dominating the accuracy–cost trade-off across all active spaces above CAS(6,6), where the two methods tie at the saturated FCI space.

Three near-term applications emerge directly from the benchmark results. The favorable scaling exponent (αNQS=0.089\alpha_{\mathrm{NQS}}=0.089) suggests the method can extend to substantially larger active spaces with manageable determinant growth, and the dual-channel architecture admits natural extensions to several settings of current interest. (i) Strongly correlated transition-metal chemistry. Fe–S clusters 55, 35 and metal dimers such as Cr2 43 are canonical multireference benchmarks where the compactness gain should be most consequential—the determinant tail exhibits the strongest combinatorial growth there, precisely the regime in which HI-NQS’s scaling advantage compounds fastest. The recent classical solution of the FeMo-cofactor model to chemical accuracy via DMRG and coupled cluster 57 redefines the frontier for tractable active-space targets; the ∼76\sim\!76-orbital active space treated there is squarely within the regime where HI-NQS’s compounding determinant advantage should be decisive. (ii) Larger Gaussian basis sets. Extending from the cc-pVDZ basis used here to cc-pVTZ and beyond would test whether the scaling exponent carries through toward the complete basis-set limit. (iii) Bond-breaking and dissociation studies. Potential energy surface scans through dissociation regimes are a natural target for the dual-channel architecture’s explicit spin-coupling structure. (iv) Quantum-classical hybrid implementations. Active spaces such as the iron–molybdenum cofactor of nitrogenase—a long-standing benchmark for fault-tolerant quantum algorithms 34—motivate workflows in which a classical Transformer sampler provides high-quality reference states that reduce the circuit depth required for quantum diagonalization. By preserving the handover mechanism of HI-VQE 31, 55, HI-NQS retains a natural interface to future quantum-circuit samplers, where the classical Transformer can serve as either a noise-resilient baseline or a warm-start initialization for shorter-depth circuit-sampled SQD 35, 56.

More broadly, these benchmarks point to a structural shift: as active-space size grows, a classical generative sampler with inductive bias matched to fermionic spin structure can outpace perturbatively ordered SCI methods in basis compactness, suggesting that the gap between selected-CI and neural quantum states is a matter of architecture rather than principle. Recent NQS+SCI methods—NQS-SC 41, HAAR-SCI 58, ARNN-SCI 47, GTNN-SCI 19, and the QiankunNet family 53, 38, 43—are converging on a shared design principle: explicit feedback between a generative sampler and exact subspace diagonalization. Scaling-law analyses of Transformer-based NQS suggest that this class of ansatz has not yet reached its performance ceiling as a function of model size and active-space dimension 22, reinforcing the case for continued architectural investment. HI-NQS contributes to this convergence by demonstrating that an inductive bias matched to the spin structure of fermionic Hamiltonians, when coupled to factorized eigenvector supervision, yields a sub-CIPSI scaling exponent on GPU hardware without any quantum-hardware resource. HI-NQS thus stands as a practical classical algorithm for strongly correlated quantum chemistry that preserves a direct interface to future hybrid classical–quantum workflows.
